h41.content:
Pope Pius IX convened the twentieth ecumenical council in 1869. Its constitution Dei Filius taught the harmony of faith and reason, and Pastor Aeternus defined papal primacy and the infallibility of the pope when he speaks ex cathedra on faith and morals.

The council was suspended when Italian troops captured Rome in 1870, ending the Papal States.

h42.content:
Responding to the hardships of the Industrial Revolution, Pope Leo XIII issued Rerum Novarum, "On the Condition of Labor." It defended private property and rejected socialism, but also insisted on just wages, workers’ right to organize, and the duty of the state to protect the poor.

It began the modern tradition of Catholic social teaching, developed by later popes in encyclicals such as Quadragesimo Anno, Centesimus Annus, and Laudato Si’.

h43.content:
From May to October 1917, the Virgin Mary appeared six times to three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, at Fatima, Portugal. She asked for daily recitation of the Rosary, penance, and the consecration of Russia to her Immaculate Heart.

On October 13, tens of thousands of people reported the "Miracle of the Sun." The Church approved the apparitions in 1930.

h44.content:
Since 1870 the popes had considered themselves prisoners in the Vatican. In 1929 the Holy See and Italy signed the Lateran Treaty, recognizing Vatican City as an independent sovereign state.

The tiny state, about 110 acres, guarantees the pope’s independence from any national government.

h45.content:
Pope Pius XI’s encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (1937), smuggled into Germany and read from pulpits, condemned Nazi ideology. During the war, the Church sheltered many Jews in convents, monasteries, and the Vatican itself. Pius XII’s public restraint remains debated by historians.

Many Catholics died in the camps, including St. Maximilian Kolbe and St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein), and some 2,500 priests were imprisoned at Dachau.

h46.content:
On November 1, 1950, Pope Pius XII solemnly defined that the Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.

It was the most recent exercise of papal infallibility. The Assumption had been celebrated by Christians of East and West for well over a thousand years before its definition.

h47.content:
Karol Wojtyła of Kraków was elected in 1978 as the first non-Italian pope in 455 years. His first visit to communist Poland in 1979 inspired the Solidarity movement, which helped bring down communism in Eastern Europe in 1989.

He visited 129 countries, founded World Youth Day, canonized more saints than all his predecessors combined, and promulgated the Catechism of the Catholic Church. His pontificate was the third longest in history.

h48.content:
Requested by the 1985 Synod of Bishops and prepared under the direction of Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, the Catechism was promulgated by John Paul II in 1992, with the definitive Latin edition in 1997.

Its four parts cover the Creed, the sacraments, the moral life, and prayer. It was the first universal catechism since the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent.

h49.content:
Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger was elected as Benedict XVI in 2005. In 2013 he became the first pope in nearly 600 years to resign. His successor, Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires, took the name Francis, becoming the first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope.

Francis died on Easter Monday, April 21, 2025, during the Jubilee Year of Hope. On May 8, 2025, Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost, an Augustinian from Chicago who had served for many years in Peru, was elected as Pope Leo XIV, the first pope from the United States.

h50.content:
According to an ancient Spanish tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared to St. James the Greater while he was discouraged by his slow progress preaching in Spain. She was said to be standing on a pillar of jasper by the Ebro River at Zaragoza. She encouraged him and asked for a church to be built there.

If the tradition is true, this would be the only apparition during Mary’s earthly life. The Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar still enshrines the pillar, and her feast on October 12 is Spain’s national day of Hispanic heritage.

h51.content:
According to tradition, the Saxon noblewoman Richeldis de Faverches had a vision of the Virgin Mary in 1061 at Walsingham in Norfolk. She was shown the house at Nazareth where the Annunciation took place and asked to build a replica in England.

"England’s Nazareth" became one of the greatest shrines of medieval Europe until Henry VIII destroyed it in 1538. Pilgrimage revived in the late 19th century, and today both Catholic and Anglican shrines stand in the village.

h52.content:
Carmelite tradition holds that in 1251 the Virgin Mary appeared to St. Simon Stock, prior general of the Carmelites, in Cambridge, England. She is said to have given him the brown scapular as a sign of her protection.

The brown scapular, two small pieces of wool worn over the shoulders, became one of the most widespread Catholic devotions. The feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel is kept on July 16.

h53.content:
In December 1531, the Virgin Mary appeared four times to St. Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert, on the hill of Tepeyac outside Mexico City. She spoke to him in his native Nahuatl and asked for a church. As a sign for the bishop, she had him gather roses from the winter hillside in his tilma (cloak).

When he opened the tilma before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga, an image of Mary was imprinted on it. The image, showing Mary as a pregnant young woman clothed with the sun, hangs in the Basilica of Guadalupe, one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world. Millions of Indigenous people were baptized in the following decades. She is patroness of the Americas.

h54.content:
In the French Alps, the Virgin Mary appeared to Benoîte Rencurel, a poor and unschooled shepherdess, beginning in 1664 and continuing, by her account, for over fifty years. Mary asked her to build a church and a house for priests "for the conversion of sinners."

The shrine at Laus became known for the sacrament of Confession and for healings attributed to oil from its sanctuary lamp. The local bishop formally recognized the apparitions in 2008, the first approval in France since Lourdes.

h55.content:
In 1830, St. Catherine Labouré, a novice with the Daughters of Charity, saw the Virgin Mary several times in the chapel of her convent on the Rue du Bac in Paris. Mary showed her the design of a medal bearing the prayer "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee."

The medal spread rapidly amid cholera epidemics. So many graces were attributed to it that people began calling it the "Miraculous Medal." Its prayer helped prepare for the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854.

h56.content:
On September 19, 1846, two young cowherds, Maximin Giraud and Mélanie Calvat, saw a weeping woman seated on a stone high in the French Alps. She spoke of her grief over the neglect of Sunday, blasphemy, and indifference, and warned of coming hardship unless people converted.

After investigation, the bishop of Grenoble approved the apparition in 1851. The Basilica of Our Lady of La Salette stands at the site, and the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette carry on its message of reconciliation.

h57.content:
Between February 11 and July 16, 1858, fourteen-year-old St. Bernadette Soubirous saw a young lady eighteen times in the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes. The lady asked for prayer and penance and told Bernadette to dig in the ground, where a spring appeared. On March 25 she said, "I am the Immaculate Conception."

The bishop of Tarbes approved the apparitions in 1862. Lourdes now receives millions of pilgrims a year, especially the sick. Its medical bureau has examined thousands of claimed cures, and the Church has recognized about seventy as miraculous.

h58.content:
In October 1859, a young Belgian immigrant, Adele Brise, saw a lady dressed in white near Green Bay, Wisconsin. The lady told her to pray for sinners and to "gather the children in this wild country and teach them what they should know for salvation."

Adele spent the rest of her life teaching the faith to children on the frontier. In 1871, when the Peshtigo Fire swept the region, people who took refuge at the chapel survived. In 2010 the bishop of Green Bay approved the apparitions, the first in the United States to receive formal approval.

h59.content:
On the evening of January 17, 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War, as Prussian troops approached the village of Pontmain, several children saw the Virgin Mary in the night sky. She was dressed in blue with golden stars, and a message appeared beneath her: "But pray, my children. God will hear you in a short time."

The Prussian advance halted that night, and an armistice followed days later. The bishop of Laval approved the apparition in 1872.

h60.content:
On the rainy evening of August 21, 1879, fifteen villagers in Knock, County Mayo, saw a silent apparition at the gable wall of their parish church. It showed the Virgin Mary, St. Joseph, and St. John the Evangelist beside an altar with a lamb and a cross. It lasted about two hours, and no words were spoken.

Knock became Ireland’s national Marian shrine. Pope St. John Paul II visited in 1979, and Pope Francis named it an international Marian and Eucharistic shrine in 2021.

h61.content:
Between November 1932 and January 1933, five children in Beauraing, Belgium, reported 33 appearances of the Virgin Mary near a convent school garden. She showed them a heart of gold and asked, "Do you love my Son? Do you love me? Then sacrifice yourselves for me."

The bishop of Namur approved the apparitions in 1949. Beauraing is known as the shrine of the "Virgin with the Golden Heart."

h62.content:
Weeks after Beauraing, eleven-year-old Mariette Beco saw a lady in white eight times near her family’s home in Banneux, Belgium. The lady called herself the "Virgin of the Poor," led Mariette to a spring "reserved for all nations," and said, "I come to relieve suffering."

The bishop of Liège approved the apparitions in 1949. Banneux draws many sick pilgrims, especially from across Europe.

h63.content:
In 1973, Sr. Agnes Katsuko Sasagawa, a deaf nun in Akita, Japan, reported messages from the Virgin Mary calling for prayer, penance, and reparation, with the Rosary. A wooden statue of Mary in the convent was reported to have wept 101 times between 1975 and 1981, witnessed by hundreds of people.

In 1984, Bishop John Shojiro Ito of Niigata declared the events worthy of belief. Sr. Agnes also recovered her hearing, which was attributed to Mary’s intercession.

h64.content:
Beginning in November 1981, several students at a girls’ school in Kibeho, Rwanda, reported apparitions of the Virgin Mary, who called herself "Mother of the Word." She called for conversion, prayer, and the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows. In one vision, the visionaries saw rivers of blood and scenes of slaughter.

Many saw these visions as a warning of the 1994 genocide, during which Kibeho itself was the site of massacres. In 2001 the bishop of Gikongoro approved the apparitions to the three principal visionaries. It is the only approved Marian apparition in Africa.

h65.content:
Since June 1981, several visionaries in the village of Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina have reported ongoing messages from the Virgin Mary, under the title "Queen of Peace." Millions of pilgrims have visited, and many report conversions, confessions, and vocations.

The Church has not declared the apparitions supernatural. In September 2024, however, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith granted a nihil obstat to the spiritual experience there. This recognizes its good fruits and permits public devotion, without ruling on whether the apparitions themselves are authentic.

h66.content:
Reports of apparitions are investigated first by the local bishop. They are examined for doctrinal soundness, the character of the visionaries, lasting spiritual fruits, and any claimed healings. Guidelines issued in 1978 were replaced in May 2024 by new norms from the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. The most favorable usual verdict is now a nihil obstat, meaning devotion is permitted and encouraged, without a formal declaration that the event is supernatural.

Even fully approved apparitions are "private revelation." Catholics are not required to believe them. As the Catechism teaches (CCC 67), they do not add to the faith but can help people live it more fully in a particular age.

h67.content:
Captured by raiders as a boy and enslaved in Ireland, Patrick escaped to Britain and later returned as a bishop, traditionally in 432. He preached across the island and ordained clergy. His Confessio is one of the few firsthand accounts from 5th-century Britain.

Within generations Ireland became a land of monasteries. Irish monks such as Columba and Columbanus later carried the faith and learning back to Scotland, England, and continental Europe.

h68.content:
Galileo Galilei’s telescope discoveries supported Copernicus’s view that the Earth moves around the Sun. After years of controversy, the Roman Inquisition condemned him in 1633 for defending heliocentrism as proven, and he spent his last years under house arrest near Florence.

The case has often been used to claim that faith and science are enemies, although the history is more complicated. In 1992, after a commission had studied the case, Pope St. John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians who judged Galileo had erred.

h69.content:
Under pressure from the Catholic monarchies of Portugal, France, and Spain, which had already expelled the Jesuits from their territories, Pope Clement XIV dissolved the Society of Jesus in 1773. Thousands of Jesuits lost their schools and missions, including the famous "reductions" of Paraguay.

The Society survived in Russia, where Catherine the Great refused to publish the papal brief. Pope Pius VII restored the Jesuits worldwide in 1814.

h70.content:
A group of Anglican clergy at Oxford, including John Henry Newman, John Keble, and Edward Pusey, sought to recover the Church of England’s Catholic heritage: apostolic succession, the sacraments, and the Church Fathers. They published their views in a series of Tracts for the Times.

Newman’s study of the early Church led him into the Catholic Church in 1845, followed by many others. The movement also transformed Anglican worship and spirituality.

h71.content:
After Christianity was banned in Japan in the early 1600s, thousands of believers kept the faith in secret for more than two centuries without priests. They baptized their children, prayed in disguised forms, and hid Marian images as Buddhist statues.

On March 17, 1865, a group of villagers approached Fr. Bernard Petitjean at the new Ōura Church in Nagasaki and whispered, "Our hearts are the same as yours." Pope Pius IX called it a miracle of the Orient.

h72.content:
When Mexico’s government strictly enforced anti-clerical laws, it expelled foreign priests, closed churches, and banned public worship. In response, Catholics rose in armed rebellion under the cry "¡Viva Cristo Rey!" ("Long live Christ the King!").

Thousands died before a negotiated settlement in 1929. Among the many martyrs are the Jesuit Bl. Miguel Pro, executed in 1927, and the teenager St. José Sánchez del Río, canonized in 2016.

h73.content:
After years of searching through philosophy and the Manichean sect, the brilliant teacher Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan when he heard a child’s voice chanting "Take up and read." He opened Paul’s Letter to the Romans and read: "put on the Lord Jesus Christ."

He was baptized by St. Ambrose at the Easter Vigil of 387, answering the prayers of his mother, St. Monica. He became one of the most influential theologians in history.

h74.content:
Regional councils in North Africa, at Hippo in 393 and at Carthage in 397, drew up a list of the books of Scripture that matches the Catholic Bible today, including the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament. The list was reaffirmed at Carthage in 419 and sent to Rome for confirmation.

These councils reflected what the Church had long read in its liturgy. Later ecumenical councils, at Florence (1442) and Trent (1546), solemnly defined the same canon.

h75.content:
The Second Council of Orange in southern Gaul settled a long debate over "semi-Pelagianism," the idea that the first step toward God comes from human effort alone. Drawing on the teaching of St. Augustine, it declared that even the beginning of faith is a gift of God’s grace.

Pope Boniface II confirmed its decrees in 531, making them a lasting reference point for Catholic teaching on grace and free will.

h76.content:
Threatened by the Lombards, Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps to seek help from Pepin the Short, king of the Franks. Pepin defeated the Lombards and granted the conquered lands of central Italy to the pope.

This "Donation of Pepin" founded the Papal States, which the popes governed for more than a thousand years, until Italian unification in 1870. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 later created Vatican City.

h77.content:
Seeking a stricter observance of the Rule of St. Benedict, St. Robert of Molesme, St. Alberic, and St. Stephen Harding founded a new monastery at Cîteaux in Burgundy. The Cistercians embraced simplicity, manual labor, and solitude.

When St. Bernard arrived in 1113 with some thirty companions, the order exploded. Within a century there were hundreds of Cistercian abbeys across Europe. The Trappists are a later reform of the same order.

h78.content:
On December 29, 1170, four knights of King Henry II murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after a long conflict over the Church’s freedom from royal control.

The killing shocked Christendom. Thomas was canonized just three years later, and the king did public penance at his tomb. Canterbury became one of Europe’s greatest pilgrimage destinations.

h79.content:
At Christmas in 1223, St. Francis of Assisi wanted to see with his own eyes the poverty in which Christ was born. In a cave at Greccio, he arranged a manger with hay, an ox, and a donkey, and Mass was celebrated there before the gathered villagers.

The practice of setting up a crèche spread throughout the Christian world and remains a beloved Christmas tradition.

h80.content:
Inspired by the visions of St. Juliana of Liège, who longed for a feast in honor of the Eucharist, Pope Urban IV established the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ for the whole Church in 1264.

The texts of the feast, including the hymns Pange Lingua and Tantum Ergo, are traditionally attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas. Eucharistic processions through the streets became one of the feast’s most beloved customs.
